evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-stricken miniature artist starts seeing her dead mother in the house she built, and a family tragedy turns into a possession nightmare that rewrites who in the Graham family is being inhabited.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean, high-recognition horror engine with a strong emotional spine: bereavement, family fracture, and escalating supernatural dread. The hook is easy to sell from the funeral-home opening through the seance and the final possession reveal, and it has obvious genre-audience pull.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script announces its concept immediately with the miniature house motif, the funeral, and Charlie’s uncanny behavior. By the time Annie finds the seance material and the sigil, the audience understands the engine: grief, occult manipulation, and a family being pulled toward a hidden ritual.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Annie is a loaded lead: artist, mother, skeptic, and someone whose control issues are inseparable from her grief. Steve and Peter are also sharply usable, especially in the dinner-table blowup and Peter’s guilt spiral after the accident, which gives the cast real acting territory.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The miniature-house visual grammar is unusually specific and gives the film its own identity from page one. The script commits hard to a slow-burn domestic horror register that keeps turning ordinary family spaces into ritual objects, which is a confident and distinctive choice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps tightening the noose: funeral, odd signs, support group, seance, accident, possession, revelation. The second half becomes especially propulsive once the family realizes the curse is active and the story starts moving toward the attic/treehouse endgame.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels fresh because the supernatural reveal is embedded in a painfully specific family drama rather than bolted onto it. The miniature art, the inherited occult history, and the final body-switching ritual all click together in a way that feels both surprising and inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The house, workshop, treehouse, support group, school, and Joan’s apartment all feel story-generating and thematically linked. The occult iconography, family history, and handmade objects create a dense world with rules and visual memory.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakable: intimate domestic realism colliding with ritualistic dread and grotesque supernatural imagery. The film knows exactly when to be quiet, when to be emotionally raw, and when to go full nightmare.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing that the family trauma is only the surface of a much older occult structure. The mother-daughter, mother-son, and inheritance threads all suggest deeper mythology without losing the immediate emotional stakes.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Annie/Steve, Annie/Peter, Annie/Charlie, and Steve/Peter all generate different kinds of pressure, and the dinner scene proves the family can carry long-form conflict. Joan adds a potent outside relationship that widens the emotional and supernatural field.

lead_characters.name: Annie Graham
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s to mid 40s, mother, artist, white, emotionally volatile but highly intelligent.
lead_characters.hook: A meticulous miniature artist and grieving mother whose need for control is both her gift and her wound. Annie is funny, prickly, defensive, and deeply loving, but her unresolved history with her mother and her own sleepwalking episode make her the perfect vessel for the film’s descent into possession and self-doubt.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is Toni Collette in Hereditary territory: a role that lets an actor pivot from brittle realism to full-body terror and then to operatic breakdown. It offers the rare showcase of playing grief, rage, denial, and supernatural possession in one sustained arc.

lead_characters.name: Steve Graham
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, husband, psychiatrist, white, controlled and professional.
lead_characters.hook: Steve is the family’s stabilizer, a calm, rational husband who keeps trying to translate catastrophe into something treatable. His restraint is both admirable and tragic, because the more he tries to manage Annie and Peter, the more powerless he becomes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Gabriel Byrne in a role like a prestige-family patriarch under siege: contained, wounded, and forced to watch reason fail in real time. It gives an actor the chance to play authority collapsing without ever becoming broad.

lead_characters.name: Peter Graham
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 17, son, high-school student, white, anxious and emotionally shut down.
lead_characters.hook: Peter is the guilt-ridden teenage son whose detachment reads as cruelty until the film reveals how much fear and self-loathing he’s carrying. He’s the most vulnerable male host in the story, and the script smartly lets his panic, shame, and dissociation build until they become the horror engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Alex Wolff a breakout showcase: a teenage performance that has to carry panic, repression, and eventual possession. It’s a demanding close-up part with real transformation and trauma work.

lead_characters.name: Charlie Graham
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 13, daughter, neurodivergent-coded, androgynous presentation, white.
lead_characters.hook: Charlie is the film’s most unsettling presence: quiet, observant, socially off-kilter, and deeply connected to the film’s handmade, death-tinged imagery. She feels like a child who is already half in another world, which makes her both heartbreaking and ominous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of eerie, unforgettable child performance that can define a young actor’s career, like a role that asks for stillness, oddity, and emotional ambiguity instead of speeches. It’s a rare part where the actor’s face and physicality do most of the work.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 60s to 70s, bereaved older woman, white, outwardly warm but increasingly uncanny.
lead_characters.hook: Joan begins as a compassionate grief-group ally and gradually reveals herself as the film’s human doorway into the occult. She’s disarming, maternal, and almost too helpful, which makes her the perfect Trojan horse for the ritual machinery underneath the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-film reveal role that gives an actor a delicious tonal pivot, similar to a prestige thriller’s hidden operator. It lets the performer play warmth, manipulation, and ceremonial authority in one package.

casting_characteristics: one teenage daughter role with unusual physicality and stillness
one teenage son role carrying heavy emotional and possession material
older-woman supporting role with a warm-to-menacing pivot

notable_requirements: family house with workshop and attic access

technical.vfx_details: Possession imagery, floating body moments, headless/decapitation effects, ant swarms, and a few supernatural movement beats; mostly practical-feeling but with some compositing and enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, fire effects, decapitation/maiming effects, flies/ants, and body-prop work for the attic and finale.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Realistic release model is specialty theatrical with strong festival launch or premium streaming horror event.

budget.note: The house, workshop, attic, treehouse, and school can be managed efficiently, but the finale adds practical gore, fire, flies/ants, and possession effects that need disciplined execution.

casting.note: The film lives or dies on Annie, and Peter/Charlie both need actors who can play strange, wounded, and specific without overplaying the horror. Joan also needs a performer who can pivot from grief-group warmth to occult authority.

development.note: The concept is clear, the escalation is legible, and the occult reveal is structurally planted. The main development conversation is not story architecture but how much supernatural ambiguity the buyer wants preserved versus clarified.

comp_set.title: The Babadook
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-driven mother-child horror story where emotional collapse and supernatural manifestation are inseparable.

comp_set.title: The Witch
comp_set.why_it_comps: Prestige horror with ritual dread, family fracture, and a patient escalation toward occult revelation.

comp_set.title: The Others
comp_set.why_it_comps: A domestic haunted-house structure that turns family space into a pressure chamber and pays off with a devastating supernatural reveal.

comp_set.title: It Comes at Night
comp_set.why_it_comps: Claustrophobic family paranoia, escalating mistrust, and a slow-burn horror register that prioritizes dread over spectacle.

comp_set.title: The Sixth Sense
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-centered supernatural mystery with a late reveal that recontextualizes the family dynamic.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult horror fans who want prestige-level dread, strong performances, and a family story that gets under the skin.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, balanced gender appeal, strongest with genre-literate viewers and prestige-horror audiences.

budget_tier.note: Mostly contained contemporary interiors with a few exterior set pieces, but the finale’s practical effects, creature-like imagery, and night work keep it above true micro territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits squarely in the lane where character-first horror can open on performance and close on nightmare imagery. The script has the kind of visual identity and emotional severity that buyers use to justify a higher-end genre play.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed, decisive ending; the power is in the one-off family tragedy and occult reveal, not an extensible universe.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The miniature-house motif is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: It gives the film a visual brand that is easy to market and hard to mistake for anything else. Buyers can sell the movie off the image of a perfect house model becoming a nightmare object, which is a real poster and trailer asset.
strengths.evidence: The opening workshop sequence and the repeated cutaways to Annie’s miniatures, especially the Graham house and the final mirrored house image.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Annie is a showcase lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The script offers a performance centerpiece that can attract serious actors and elevate the project above routine genre fare. That kind of role is a packaging lever because it can unlock both prestige credibility and horror audience interest.
strengths.evidence: The funeral eulogy, the support-group confession, the dinner-table explosion, and the possession sequence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family conflict is the engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The horror lands because the emotional stakes are already combustible before the supernatural reveal fully arrives. That makes the movie feel bigger than its locations and gives the buyer a reason to believe in word-of-mouth beyond gore.
strengths.evidence: The dinner scene, Annie and Peter’s mutual blame, and Steve’s attempts to mediate while losing control.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The occult reveal is deeply planted.
strengths.what_it_means: The script earns its escalation by layering symbols, books, photos, and ritual details before the final explanation lands. That makes the ending feel like a payoff rather than a twist for its own sake.
strengths.evidence: The sigil necklace, Joan’s apartment, the grimoire, the attic body, and the Paimon ritual text.

strengths.what_it_means: It lives in the lane buyers are actively chasing: elevated, adult, emotionally severe horror with a strong auteur feel. That makes it easier to position for festival launch, specialty theatrical, or streamer prestige genre slates.
strengths.evidence: The long quiet stretches, the grief-group scenes, the controlled domestic scenes, and the final operatic nightmare imagery.

whats_special.headline: This is a premium horror package with a built-in visual signature, a major female lead role, and a contained production footprint that still delivers event-level dread. The script’s mix of family tragedy, occult mystery, and unforgettable imagery is exactly the kind of lane buyers can market as prestige genre without needing tentpole spend.

items.area: The finale leans hard on explanation.
items.detail: Once Joan’s apartment and the attic reveal the Paimon ritual, the script shifts from dread to exposition-heavy confirmation. That’s not a fatal flaw, but it does mean the last act is more dependent on buyers liking the mythology than on pure suspense.

items.area: Annie’s arc is so dominant it narrows the ensemble.
items.detail: The film is structurally Annie’s movie, which is a strength, but it also means Steve, Peter, Charlie, and Joan are all measured against her gravitational pull. For a producer, that concentrates value in one role and makes the rest of the cast feel more functional than independently expandable.

items.area: The third act requires a lot of effects confidence.
items.detail: The headless body, floating Annie, fire transfer, ant swarm, and treehouse ritual all need to land cleanly or the movie loses authority fast. This is still manageable, but the ending is not forgiving of weak practical execution or undercooked compositing.

items.area: Peter’s possession turn is emotionally abrupt by design.
items.detail: The final body-switching move is bold, but it asks the audience to accept a big metaphysical pivot after spending most of the film inside family grief and paranoia. That makes the ending memorable, but it also means some buyers will read the last movement as a hard genre turn rather than a seamless continuation.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the concept; it’s the degree to which the movie’s payoff depends on the audience buying the occult machinery and the final possession logic. The project is strongest when it stays in family horror mode, and the buyer conversation will center on whether the mythology-heavy back half is a feature or a risk.
